newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CS chairman Gut urges action on Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: CS chairman Gut urges action on Holocaust fund.

text.p: A top Swiss banker has called for a bold stroke to restore the country's reputation amidst allegations the Swiss bankrolled Nazi Germany's war efforts and hoarded the wealth of Holocaust victims.

In an article published on Wednesday by the Neue Zuercher Zeitung (NZZ) newspaper, Credit Suisse Group chairman Rainer Gut called for establishing a fund to compensate impoverished victims of Nazi persecution and their relatives.

The fund -- a goodwill gesture financed in equal parts by the government, the Swiss National Bank and banks and insurers -- would likely have to be larger than 100 million Swiss francs ($70 million), the paper said without quoting Gut directly.

"Gut declined to comment on the exact size of the fund, but indicated that before Christmas, he had estimated around 100 million Swiss francs. In view of the events since the end of the year, the amount should be significantly larger," the NZZ said.
"Gut regards such a measure as completely in keeping with the humanitarian tradition of Switzerland," it added, estimating around 400,000 needy people of all faiths could benefit.

He was referring to the row that arose after outgoing Swiss president Jean-Pascal Delamuraz labelled Jewish groups' demands to set up a compensation fund "blackmail." Delamuraz, who is economics minister, has since apologised.
A CS spokesman confirmed Gut made the comments in a "discussion" with the newspaper.

Gut said Berne should also guarantee to cover any claims that arise from a historians' review of Switzerland's wartime role. The sweeping probe by a nine-member panel will examine whether the Swiss acted honourably during the war.
Anyone cited in the report for wrongdoing could be forced to help finance the effort retroactively, he said.

Gut, a pillar of Switzerland's financial establishment, also suggested Switzerland adopt a system in which the state takes over dormant accounts after a certain period rather than leave them at banks.
